- On the second day, every pair of participants exactly one of whom was Israeli shook hands.

### 1.  Handshakes per pair of nationalities  

| pair | days they shake hands | total handshakes |
|------|----------------------|------------------|
| Israeli – Israeli | day 1 only | \(\displaystyle\binom I2\) |
| Greek – Greek     | day 1 only | \(\displaystyle\binom G2\) |
| Japanese – Japanese| day 1 only | \(\displaystyle\binom J2\) |
| Israeli – Greek   | days 2 & 3 | \(2IG\) |
| Israeli – Japanese| day 2 only | \(IJ\) |
| Greek – Japanese  | never | \(0\) |

Hence the total number of handshakes is  

\[
T=\binom I2+\binom G2+\binom J2+IJ+2IG. \tag{2}
\]

We are told that \(T=20200\).

---

### 2.  Eliminate \(J\)

From (1) \(J=202-I-G\).  
Insert this into (2):

\[
\begin{aligned}
20200&=\frac{I(I-1)}2+\frac{G(G-1)}2
      +\frac{(202-I-G)(201-I-G)}2 \\
     &\qquad+I(202-I-G)+2IG .
\end{aligned}
\]

After expanding and simplifying one obtains a remarkably simple
expression that involves only \(I\) and \(G\):

\[
G^{2}+(2I-202)G+101=0. \tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  Integer solutions of (3)

Equation (3) is a quadratic in \(G\).  
For integer \(G\) the discriminant must be a perfect square:

\[
\Delta=(2I-202)^{2}-4\cdot101
      =4\bigl[(I-101)^{2}-101\bigr].
\]

Thus \((I-101)^{2}-101\) must itself be a perfect square, say \(k^{2}\).  
We get the Diophantine equation  

\[
(I-101)^{2}-k^{2}=101
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\bigl(I-101-k\bigr)\bigl(I-101+k\bigr)=101. \tag{4}
\]

Since \(101\) is prime, the integer factor pairs of \(101\) are  
\((1,101),\;(-1,-101)\) (the order does not matter).  

*Case 1:* \(I-101-k=1,\; I-101+k=101\)  

\[
2(I-101)=102\;\Longrightarrow\; I=152.
\]

*Case 2:* \(I-101-k=-1,\; I-101+k=-101\)  

\[
2(I-101)=-102\;\Longrightarrow\; I=50.
\]

Both \(I=152\) and \(I=50\) satisfy the discriminant condition, but we must still have a non‑negative solution for \(G\) from (3).

- For \(I=152\):  (3) becomes \(G^{2}+102G+101=0\), whose roots are
  \(-1\) and \(-101\) – not admissible.
- For \(I=50\): (3) becomes \(G^{2}-102G+101=0\), whose roots are
  \(1\) and \(101\), both non‑negative.

Thus the only feasible value is  

\[
\boxed{\,I=50\,}.
\]
